subject: Physics
scope_summary: Owner-approved ExamSIDE question-demand slice for plane motion, now semantically decomposed for the Topic Atlas: one-frame/two-component motion, componentwise constant acceleration, and the gravity-only projectile model with explicit apex, same-height and horizontal/unequal-height event reasoning. Trajectory-equation derivation, drag, variable gravity, moving-launcher/relative-motion cases and advanced projectile geometry remain outside this bounded packet.

resources.title: Grade9V3 Motion-in-2D adaptation from owner-approved ExamSIDE demand
resources.section: Independent x/y motion, 2D constant acceleration and projectile model
resources.rights_status: Author-created adaptation. External ExamSIDE questions remain linked/summarized rather than copied; no Pinnacle curriculum authority is claimed.
resources.selection_reason: Turns selected real ExamSIDE question demand into the smallest durable local learner-action spine while preserving the distinction between external question evidence and school-issued scope.

cognitive_target.target_failure: The learner treats independent x- and y-component equations as if they may use unrelated clocks and still form one physical state.
cognitive_target.target_operation: Sample x(t) and y(t) at one shared instant, then reconstruct the particle's simultaneous two-dimensional state.
cognitive_target.core_invariant: Separate component equations share one physical event clock.
cognitive_target.boundary: Values taken from different times may each be valid measurements, but they cannot be combined as one simultaneous state of the same object.

graphical_contract.phenomenon_view: One moving object with x- and y-projections that remain visibly tied to the same particle.
graphical_contract.mechanism_view: A shared time marker drives both component histories; a mixed-time pair is rendered as an invalid ghost state.
graphical_contract.mathematical_structure_view: The valid state is reconstructed as r(t)=(x(t),y(t)); x(t1),y(t2) with t1≠t2 is not one physical state.
graphical_contract.direct_manipulation: Split or synchronize the x and y time controls.
causal_chain: one object defines one event time
both components must be sampled at that time
same-time samples form one valid state
mixed-time samples create a ghost state
graphical_contract.progressive_disclosure: Show the object and clocks before revealing the invariant; reveal the ghost-state explanation only after an invalid combination is attempted.
graphical_contract.counterfactual_model: Allow t_x and t_y to differ so the learner can construct the tempting but physically invalid mixed-time state.

boundary_contract.assumption_held: Both components describe the same object and the same physical event.
boundary_contract.stress_action: Deliberately sample x at one time and y at another.
boundary_contract.expected_break: The ordered pair no longer corresponds to any simultaneous state the particle occupied.
boundary_contract.learner_must_identify: Independence belongs to the component equations, not to the physical clock.

state_fidelity_contract.source_of_truth: The authoritative state is the pair of component clock values, their synchronization status, x(t_x), y(t_y), and whether the reconstructed ordered pair is a valid simultaneous particle state.
state_fidelity_contract.unit_constant_policy: Time units and the x(t), y(t) coordinate units must be shared by both component histories and the reconstructed particle readout; no representation may apply an independent conversion.
state_fidelity_contract.reset_policy: Reset must return both component clocks to the documented common initial instant, clear any ghost-state mismatch, and redraw the particle and both histories from that same state.

resources.title: Independent Components, One Shared Clock Explorer
resources.section: Two component histories, one physical object and one shared event clock
resources.selection_reason: Interactive repair surface for the misconception that independent component equations imply independent physical clocks.

cognitive_target.target_failure: The learner solves separate x- and y-times for what is actually one physical event such as impact, apex, or crossing a wall.
cognitive_target.target_operation: Use the component that defines the event to determine t_event, then sample every other component at that same time.
cognitive_target.core_invariant: A physical event has one time even when one axis supplies the easiest event condition.
cognitive_target.boundary: Different named events may occur at different times; the shared-time rule applies to all coordinates of the same event, not to unrelated events.

graphical_contract.phenomenon_view: A trajectory with a named event such as impact, apex, or wall crossing highlighted before equations are solved.
graphical_contract.mechanism_view: One event-time marker cuts through both component histories and shows that the axis finding time does not own a separate clock.
graphical_contract.mathematical_structure_view: The event condition yields t_event; x(t_event) and y(t_event) then reconstruct the event state.
graphical_contract.direct_manipulation: Choose the event and deliberately choose the time used on the other axis.
causal_chain: event condition identifies when the event occurs
that solution defines t_event
the same t_event samples every component
the sampled components locate the one event
graphical_contract.progressive_disclosure: Reveal the event condition first, then event time, then force the learner to choose whether the other axis reuses it.
graphical_contract.counterfactual_model: Permit a second horizontal time to be chosen and show that it samples a different instant rather than the named event.

boundary_contract.assumption_held: The x and y calculations refer to the same named physical event.
boundary_contract.stress_action: Choose a second time for the other axis after t_event is already known.
boundary_contract.expected_break: The second component is sampled at a different instant and no longer locates the requested event.
boundary_contract.learner_must_identify: The event owns the time; an axis only provides a convenient equation for finding it.

state_fidelity_contract.source_of_truth: The authoritative state is the selected named physical event and its solved t_event; the trajectory highlight and every component evaluation must sample that same event time.
state_fidelity_contract.unit_constant_policy: The event-time unit and the units used by every component function must agree, and any event marker must be recomputed from the same t_event rather than a separately stored display value.
state_fidelity_contract.reset_policy: Reset must restore the default named event, recompute its event time, and resample both components from that one time instead of merely resetting visible selectors.

resources.section: One axis may determine event time; every component is sampled at that same instant
resources.selection_reason: Interactive repair surface for solving separate event times on x and y instead of sharing the time of one physical event.

cognitive_target.target_failure: The learner classifies an object as an ideal projectile because it was launched or follows a curved path, without checking post-release interactions.
cognitive_target.target_operation: Audit the interactions that remain after release and choose the ideal projectile specialization only for gravity-only free flight.
cognitive_target.core_invariant: For the ideal near-Earth projectile model with +y upward, a_x=0 and a_y=-g because gravity is the only retained interaction.
cognitive_target.boundary: Active thrust, significant drag, or continuing contact invalidates the ideal gravity-only specialization even if the path remains curved.

graphical_contract.phenomenon_view: Visually similar launched objects are shown so trajectory shape cannot be used as the deciding cue.
graphical_contract.mechanism_view: Post-release interaction arrows are toggled and inspected before the acceleration model is unlocked.
graphical_contract.mathematical_structure_view: The interaction audit maps to ΣF_x and ΣF_y, yielding a_x=0 and a_y=-g only in the gravity-only case.
graphical_contract.direct_manipulation: Toggle thrust, drag, and contact interactions after release.
causal_chain: inspect post-release interactions
gravity-only implies zero horizontal net force
therefore a_x=0 while gravity gives a_y=-g
extra interactions require a more general model
graphical_contract.progressive_disclosure: Hide projectile equations until the learner has inspected the active interactions.
graphical_contract.counterfactual_model: Turn thrust or drag on while keeping a projectile-like path so the learner sees that appearance does not authorize the ideal model.

boundary_contract.assumption_held: After release, gravity is the only retained force in the model.
boundary_contract.stress_action: Activate thrust, significant drag, or continuing contact.
boundary_contract.expected_break: The ideal projectile specialization no longer determines the component accelerations.
boundary_contract.learner_must_identify: The model is selected from interactions after release, not from the appearance of the trajectory.

state_fidelity_contract.source_of_truth: The authoritative state is the active set of post-release interactions; it must drive the force view, model-status gate, component accelerations, trajectory assumptions, and whether projectile equations are unlocked.
state_fidelity_contract.unit_constant_policy: Force, mass, gravitational-field and acceleration quantities must use one declared unit system, with the same gravity magnitude and sign convention feeding both the interaction audit and acceleration readouts.
state_fidelity_contract.reset_policy: Reset must restore the documented default interaction set and recompute model eligibility, force arrows, acceleration components, and equation visibility from that interaction state.

resources.title: Is It Really a Projectile? Explorer
resources.section: Post-release interaction audit before the ideal gravity-only projectile specialization
resources.selection_reason: Interactive model-selection surface that classifies projectile motion from retained interactions rather than path shape.

cognitive_target.target_failure: The learner interprets the highest point as a place where the projectile stops and gravity or acceleration becomes zero.
cognitive_target.target_operation: Separate horizontal and vertical velocity components from acceleration and identify the apex as the zero crossing of v_y.
cognitive_target.core_invariant: At the apex v_y=0 while a_y=-g; for an oblique launch with nonzero u_x, v_x remains nonzero.
cognitive_target.boundary: For a purely vertical launch u_x=0, total velocity may be zero at the top even though acceleration remains -g.

graphical_contract.phenomenon_view: A projectile is scrubbed continuously through its highest point without visually pausing horizontal motion.
graphical_contract.mechanism_view: Velocity components and the downward acceleration are displayed simultaneously before, at, and after the apex.
graphical_contract.mathematical_structure_view: The apex is identified by v_y=0 while v_x stays constant in the ideal model and a_y remains -g.
graphical_contract.direct_manipulation: Scrub the motion time across the apex.
causal_chain: gravity continuously decreases v_y
v_y reaches zero at the turning point
gravity continues acting so v_y becomes negative
horizontal velocity remains unchanged in the ideal model
graphical_contract.progressive_disclosure: Prediction should precede the apex readout; the full component state is revealed only after the learner commits.
graphical_contract.counterfactual_model: Let the learner test the idea that acceleration becomes zero at the top and compare it with the unchanged downward gravity state.

boundary_contract.assumption_held: The example is an ideal oblique projectile with nonzero horizontal component.
boundary_contract.stress_action: Set the horizontal launch component to zero and inspect the vertical turning point.
boundary_contract.expected_break: The statement 'total velocity is nonzero at the apex' no longer holds, while a_y=-g still does.
boundary_contract.learner_must_identify: The universal turning-point condition is v_y=0 with downward acceleration; nonzero total velocity additionally requires u_x≠0.

state_fidelity_contract.source_of_truth: The authoritative state is one projectile state at the scrubbed time t; trajectory position, v_x, v_y, acceleration, speed, and apex status must all be derived from that same instant.
state_fidelity_contract.unit_constant_policy: The same gravity value, time unit, coordinate scale, and velocity units must feed trajectory position, v_y evolution, speed magnitude and apex detection; no apex-only constant may diverge.
state_fidelity_contract.reset_policy: Reset must restore the documented launch state and scrub time, then recompute position, velocity components, acceleration, speed, and apex indicator from the reset time.

resources.title: The Apex Fallacy Explorer
resources.section: Apex state: v_y=0 while horizontal velocity and downward acceleration remain
resources.selection_reason: Interactive repair surface separating a zero vertical component from zero total velocity or zero acceleration.

cognitive_target.target_failure: The learner concludes that returning to the same height means returning to the same velocity or complete motion state.
cognitive_target.target_operation: Compare signed velocity components, magnitude, direction, position, and acceleration at paired equal-height events.
cognitive_target.core_invariant: On the same ideal trajectory, equal-height ascent/descent points have equal v_x, opposite v_y, equal speed, and different velocity vectors.
cognitive_target.boundary: The symmetry is not guaranteed for strong drag, unrelated projectiles, or points that do not belong to the same ideal trajectory.

graphical_contract.phenomenon_view: Two selectable points on the same trajectory are constrained to equal height, one on ascent and one on descent.
graphical_contract.mechanism_view: Signed component arrows expose that only the vertical component reverses while the horizontal component is unchanged.
graphical_contract.mathematical_structure_view: Equal |v_y| plus equal v_x gives equal speed magnitude, while opposite sign of v_y makes the vectors unequal.
graphical_contract.direct_manipulation: Move the ascent time and observe the automatically paired equal-height descent state.
causal_chain: same ideal trajectory and equal height give equal vertical-speed magnitude
v_x remains constant
ascent and descent require opposite signs of v_y
equal magnitude but different direction means same speed, different velocity
graphical_contract.progressive_disclosure: Show paired points and components before announcing the same-speed conclusion.
graphical_contract.counterfactual_model: Compare a strong-drag or unrelated-trajectory case to show that equal height alone does not guarantee the symmetry.

boundary_contract.assumption_held: Both points lie on the same gravity-only trajectory with negligible drag.
boundary_contract.stress_action: Introduce drag or compare states from different trajectories.
boundary_contract.expected_break: Equal-height speed symmetry is no longer guaranteed by the original ideal-model reasoning.
boundary_contract.learner_must_identify: The symmetry belongs to the same ideal trajectory, not to height equality in isolation.

state_fidelity_contract.source_of_truth: The authoritative state is the chosen ascent event plus its computed equal-height descent partner on the same ideal trajectory; both markers, signed components, resultant vectors and speed comparison derive from that pair.
state_fidelity_contract.unit_constant_policy: Both paired events must share one coordinate and velocity unit system, and each speed magnitude must be recomputed from its displayed signed components rather than stored independently.
state_fidelity_contract.reset_policy: Reset must restore the documented ascent event, recompute the matching descent event, and rebuild both component/vector readouts and the equal-speed comparison from the paired states.

resources.title: Same Height, Same Speed ≠ Same Velocity Explorer
resources.section: Compare ascent and descent states at equal height by signed components
resources.selection_reason: Interactive vector-state comparison showing equal speed but different velocity direction at equal-height events.

cognitive_target.target_failure: The learner applies same-height projectile shortcuts or sets u_y=0 merely because the landing height differs from the launch height.
cognitive_target.target_operation: Read the actual event geometry as Δy=y_f-y_i, retain the actual initial u_y, solve the vertical event, then reuse that time horizontally.
cognitive_target.core_invariant: The gravity-only component laws stay fixed while the landing event condition changes with signed Δy.
cognitive_target.boundary: The same-height shortcut is valid only when y_f=y_i; horizontal launch is a separate initial-condition special case with u_y=0.

graphical_contract.phenomenon_view: The landing platform is moved above, level with, or below the launch point while the launch state remains fixed.
graphical_contract.mechanism_view: The geometry panel updates y_i, y_f, signed Δy, event time, and the same-height shortcut status together.
graphical_contract.mathematical_structure_view: Δy=u_y t-(1/2)gt² keeps its form; changing y_f changes the event condition while u_y remains the actual launch component.
causal_chain: moving the landing surface changes y_f
therefore signed Δy changes
the vertical event equation gives a different t_event
the same t_event changes horizontal range
graphical_contract.progressive_disclosure: Show geometry and signed displacement before revealing whether a memorized same-height shortcut is valid.
graphical_contract.counterfactual_model: Force Δy=0 for a lower landing and show that the equation finds a real same-height-return event rather than the requested impact.

boundary_contract.assumption_held: The same-height shortcut assumes launch and landing heights are equal.
boundary_contract.stress_action: Move the landing surface away from the launch height while keeping the launch velocity unchanged.
boundary_contract.expected_break: Δy=0 no longer identifies the requested landing event even though the projectile equations themselves remain valid.
boundary_contract.learner_must_identify: u_y describes the initial velocity; Δy describes event geometry, and neither determines the other.

state_fidelity_contract.source_of_truth: The authoritative state is the fixed launch state together with the movable landing-surface height; signed Δy, vertical event equation, impact time, impact marker and horizontal range all derive from those values.
state_fidelity_contract.unit_constant_policy: Launch and landing heights, signed Δy, u_y, g, event time and horizontal range must use one declared unit/constant convention, with the same g feeding both the vertical event solver and trajectory.
state_fidelity_contract.reset_policy: Reset must restore the documented launch and landing heights, recompute signed Δy and event time, and redraw the impact and range from that recomputed geometry.

buckets.title: Two-dimensional kinematics and projectile model
buckets.badge_reason: The main difficulty is keeping one coordinate frame and one time variable while treating perpendicular components independently and selecting the projectile specialization only when its assumptions hold.

scope.covers: Independent perpendicular component motion in one frame, constant-acceleration component equations with common time, and the ideal near-Earth projectile specialization for horizontal and oblique launch questions.
excluded: Calculus-based differentiation of a time-dependent position vector.
Derivation or memorization of a large catalogue of range/height/time-of-flight formulas as separate capabilities.
Trajectory-equation derivation as a first-slice requirement.
Air drag, Coriolis effects, variable gravity, target-on-incline projectile geometry and other advanced variants.

conventions.statement: Use one declared non-rotating x-y frame for the whole event; both component equations use the same elapsed time.
When +y is chosen upward, the ideal projectile model uses a_x=0 and a_y=-g after release.

capabilities.action: Represent one plane-motion event as independent signed x/y component histories that share one elapsed time.
capabilities.success_criterion: Declares one frame, separates x and y quantities without mixing axes, uses the same time for both component states, and reconstructs the requested plane vector/position from the component pair.

capabilities.action: Apply constant-acceleration kinematics independently to x and y components of one plane-motion event.
capabilities.success_criterion: Checks that a_x and a_y are constant, writes the appropriate one-dimensional relation separately on each axis with one common t, solves only the needed components, and recombines them consistently.

capabilities.action: Recognize and solve an ideal near-Earth projectile as a special two-dimensional constant-acceleration state.
capabilities.success_criterion: After release with air resistance neglected, sets a_x=0 and a_y=-g for +y upward, keeps one common time, accepts horizontal or already-resolved oblique initial components, and reconstructs the requested speed, direction, displacement, range, height or flight-time consequence without treating those outputs as separate physical laws.

microtopics.title: Split one plane-motion event into independent x/y components with one clock
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often interpret independent components as unrelated motions and accidentally use different times or mix x and y quantities.
entry_assumptions: Can read signed vector components in a declared x-y frame.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Perpendicular components may be solved separately because each axis equation contains only that axis's quantities, but they still describe one object at one physical time.

teaching_path.action: Choose one fixed x-y frame, one origin and one time origin for the whole plane-motion event.
teaching_path.why_valid: A component value is meaningful only after its frame and sign convention are fixed.
teaching_path.output: one declared frame, origin, axis orientation and t=0

teaching_path.action: Represent position, velocity and acceleration as signed x and y components in that same frame.
teaching_path.why_valid: A plane vector is completely represented by its perpendicular Cartesian components once the frame is declared.

teaching_path.action: Keep x-quantities in the x description and y-quantities in the y description while using one shared elapsed time.
teaching_path.why_valid: The perpendicular component equations are independent in Cartesian kinematics, but both describe the same object during the same physical interval.
teaching_path.output: two axis histories coupled by one clock

teaching_path.action: Recombine only component values that refer to the same frame and the same instant.
teaching_path.why_valid: Mixing x at one time with y at another does not describe any single physical state of the object.
teaching_path.output: one physically valid plane state reconstructed from simultaneous components

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Independent x and y motions may use different elapsed times.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: At one instant 2 s after launch, may the x equation use t=2 s while the y equation uses another time?
misconceptions.repair: No. Independence separates the axis equations; it does not give the same object two clocks.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The x-motion and y-motion are two different objects that can be paired arbitrarily later.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: May x(2 s) be combined with y(3 s) to describe the particle's position?
misconceptions.repair: No. A plane state is a simultaneous pair. Recombine x(t) and y(t) only at the same t in the same frame.

exit_task.prompt: A particle has x-velocity 6 m/s and y-velocity -8 m/s at t=3 s. Explain what 'independent components' means and what must remain shared between the x and y descriptions.

answer.summary: The x and y component equations are solved separately in the same frame, but both describe the same particle at the same t=3 s.
reasoning: Keep x quantities in the x equation and y quantities in the y equation.
Use one common elapsed time for the same physical instant.
Recombine components only after each axis is handled consistently.
answer.check: Both component values must refer to the same frame and same instant.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: No new numerical computation is required.

microtopics.research_contribution: ExamSIDE includes real x-y motion and projectile questions whose demand cannot be represented honestly by a one-dimensional capability alone.

predict.prompt: If x and y components are independent, does that mean the object has two different clocks?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The component equations are separate, but the event uses one common elapsed time.

attempt.produces: A two-column x/y setup with one shared t.

rubric.criterion: Axes are kept separate while time/frame remain shared.

accepted: Separate x and y equations; same t for both.
rejected: Use x acceleration in the y equation or assign unrelated times.

route.ask: What must be declared before any component can have a sign?
route.why_this_ask: Recovers the common frame and axis convention.

route.ask: What separates between axes, and what must stay common because both descriptions belong to one event?
route.why_this_ask: Distinguishes component independence from the shared-clock invariant.

route.ask: Which x and y values may be recombined into one state?
route.why_this_ask: Makes simultaneity observable rather than implicit.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: Teaching states the independence/common-time rule; reconstruction makes the learner distinguish what separates from what stays shared.

boundary_test.prompt: If a_x=0 but a_y is nonzero, may v_x stay constant while v_y changes?
boundary_test.answer: Yes. That is exactly what independent component evolution permits.
boundary_test.confirms: One component can change while the other does not.

microtopics.title: Apply constant-acceleration kinematics component by component
microtopics.badge_reason: The formulas are familiar from 1D, but the challenge is selecting the right component equation on each axis and enforcing one common time.
entry_assumptions: Can use the existing one-dimensional constant-acceleration model.
Can keep x/y components separate with one common time.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The one-dimensional constant-acceleration equations can be applied to each perpendicular component independently when a_x and a_y are each constant over the same interval.

teaching_path.action: Check separately whether a_x and a_y are constant over the interval before choosing constant-acceleration equations on either axis.
teaching_path.why_valid: The familiar one-dimensional kinematic relations are exact only on an axis whose acceleration component is constant over the interval.

teaching_path.action: Apply the one-dimensional constant-acceleration relations independently to x and y using only that axis's signed values and the same t.
teaching_path.why_valid: Each Cartesian component obeys the same one-dimensional relation when its acceleration component is constant.
teaching_path.output: v_x=u_x+a_x t; v_y=u_y+a_y t; Delta x=u_x t+0.5a_x t^2; Delta y=u_y t+0.5a_y t^2

teaching_path.action: If one axis determines an event time, reuse that same time on the other axis before recombining and checking the plane state.
teaching_path.why_valid: The event occurs once for the object; a time obtained from one component is the clock value for every component at that same event.
teaching_path.output: event time transferred across axes, then one checked plane state

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The magnitude of acceleration should be inserted unchanged into both x and y equations.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If a=(10 i + 4 j) m/s², should both component equations use a=√116?
misconceptions.repair: No. Use a_x=10 only in the x equation and a_y=4 only in the y equation; the magnitude is not either component.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If one acceleration component is constant, the constant-acceleration equations are automatically valid on both axes.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If a_x is constant but a_y changes with time, may the same constant-acceleration displacement formula be used exactly on y over the whole interval?
misconceptions.repair: No. Model validity is checked per axis. A constant a_x does not make a_y constant.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A time found from the x equation may be replaced by a different convenient time in the y equation.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If x-motion says an event occurs at t=3 s, what time belongs in the y equation for that same event?
misconceptions.repair: Use t=3 s. Both components describe the same event and therefore share one clock.

exit_task.prompt: A particle starts with u=(0,5) m/s and constant a=(10,4) m/s². Set up the x and y position equations at common time t without solving a particular numerical t.

answer.summary: Use Delta x=0*t+0.5(10)t² and Delta y=5t+0.5(4)t² with the same t.
reasoning: Read signed component initial velocities and accelerations.
Apply the 1D constant-acceleration displacement relation separately.
Keep one common elapsed time.
answer.check: Units are metres on both displacements and no x quantity appears in the y equation or vice versa.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The task asks for exact symbolic setup, not a new numerical claim.

microtopics.research_contribution: Directly matches ExamSIDE 2020 x-y constant-acceleration demand while reusing the existing 1D constant-acceleration capability rather than duplicating it.

predict.prompt: If a_x is nonzero and a_y is zero, which velocity component changes with time?
predict.defensible_answer: Only v_x changes; v_y remains constant.

attempt.produces: Two correct component constant-acceleration equations using one t.

rubric.criterion: Each axis uses only its own signed initial values and acceleration while sharing the same time.
rubric.evidence_of: 2D component model use rather than a scalar-magnitude shortcut.

accepted: v_x=u_x+a_x t and v_y=u_y+a_y t with one t.
rejected: Use |a| in both equations or use separate unrelated times.

route.ask: Before using a constant-acceleration formula, what must be true about that axis's acceleration component?
route.why_this_ask: Makes model validity explicit rather than formula-driven.

route.ask: What does the 1D relation become when written only along x, and what changes for y?
route.why_this_ask: Transfers an existing model one axis at a time.

route.ask: If one component equation finds the event time, what time must the other component use?
route.why_this_ask: Recovers the shared-clock coupling at an event.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: Teaching supplies component forms; reconstruction derives them by applying the existing 1D model separately to each axis.

boundary_test.prompt: If a_y changes with time while a_x stays constant, may the constant-acceleration equations still be exact on both axes for the whole interval?
boundary_test.answer: No. The x relation may remain exact, but the y constant-acceleration relation is not exact over that interval.
boundary_test.confirms: Model validity is checked per component.

microtopics.title: Select the gravity-only projectile model before using projectile consequences
microtopics.badge_reason: Projectile formulas become brittle when the learner skips the model decision, mixes times, or treats horizontal velocity as requiring a continuing horizontal force.
entry_assumptions: If an oblique launch angle is given, angle-based vector decomposition is available as a separate prerequisite for that question.
microtopics.inferential_jump: After release in the ideal near-Earth model, projectile motion is not a new set of laws: it is the same component kinematics with a_x=0 and a_y=-g (for +y upward).

teaching_path.action: Decide whether the object is in ideal near-Earth free flight after release; neglect air resistance, declare +y, then set a_x=0 and a_y=-g.
teaching_path.why_valid: The standard projectile equations are a conditional specialization of 2D constant acceleration, not an automatic label for every launched object.

teaching_path.action: Use supplied or separately resolved u_x and u_y with one common t in the horizontal and vertical component equations.
teaching_path.why_valid: Horizontal, oblique and downward/upward initial components change the initial state, not the gravity-only model.
teaching_path.output: v_x=u_x; v_y=u_y-g t; Delta x=u_x t; Delta y=u_y t-0.5g t^2

teaching_path.action: Translate the requested event into the component condition that defines it before solving for time.
teaching_path.why_valid: Apex, same-height return, ground impact and a specified later instant are different events; each is identified by a different component condition.

teaching_path.action: For an apex event, set v_y=0 while keeping v_x=u_x and a_y=-g.
teaching_path.why_valid: At the highest point only the vertical velocity component is momentarily zero; gravity still accelerates downward and horizontal motion continues.
teaching_path.output: apex condition v_y=0 with nonzero horizontal velocity and nonzero downward acceleration

teaching_path.action: For a return to the launch height, set Delta y=0 and treat any same-height flight-time/range shortcut as conditional on that equality.
teaching_path.why_valid: The shortcut follows from the vertical displacement returning to its initial value; it is not valid when the landing height differs.
teaching_path.output: same-height event condition and its validity boundary

teaching_path.action: For any unequal-height landing, use the actual Delta y=y_f-y_i in the vertical position equation and retain the actual u_y; for a horizontal launch specifically, set u_y=0, then obtain the event time vertically and share it with x.
teaching_path.why_valid: Initial vertical velocity and landing displacement describe different facts. The landing event is fixed by the actual vertical geometry, while u_y=0 is only the horizontal-launch initial condition.
teaching_path.output: Delta y=y_f-y_i=u_y t_event-0.5g t_event^2; for horizontal launch u_y=0; reuse the solved t_event on x

teaching_path.action: At the selected event time, reconstruct the requested velocity, speed, direction, displacement or range from simultaneous components and check qualitative limits.
teaching_path.why_valid: The reported projectile result is a consequence of one component model and one event, so its components must refer to the same instant and satisfy a_x=0, a_y=-g.
teaching_path.output: checked projectile consequence at one physical event

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A projectile needs a horizontal force to keep moving horizontally.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If a_x=0 after release, can v_x still be nonzero?
misconceptions.repair: Yes. Zero horizontal acceleration means horizontal velocity stays constant, not that it becomes zero.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A horizontal launch has no vertical velocity throughout the flight.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: One second after a horizontal launch, is v_y still zero under gravity?
misconceptions.repair: No. u_y=0 only at release; a_y=-g makes v_y=-gt afterward.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: At the highest point the whole velocity and the acceleration are both zero.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: At the apex of an oblique projectile, which of v_x, v_y and a_y is zero?
misconceptions.repair: Only v_y is zero at that instant. v_x remains u_x and a_y remains -g.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Same-height flight formulas may be used whenever the question is about a projectile range or flight time.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A ball launched from a roof lands on the ground below. May the same-height time-of-flight shortcut be used without checking the vertical displacement?
misconceptions.repair: No. Same-height shortcuts require Delta y=0 between launch and landing. For unequal heights, solve the vertical position condition.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: At two points of the same height on an ideal trajectory, the velocity vectors are identical.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: On ascent and descent at the same height, how do the horizontal and vertical velocity components compare?
misconceptions.repair: v_x is the same, while v_y has equal magnitude and opposite sign; the speed matches but the velocity vector does not.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Horizontal speed determines how long a horizontally launched object takes to fall.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the horizontal launch speed doubles from the same height, does the ideal fall time change?
misconceptions.repair: No. The vertical position equation determines the fall time; horizontal speed changes the range, not the fall time.

exit_task.prompt: A stone is launched horizontally from a cliff with speed u. With +y upward and air resistance neglected, write its component acceleration, velocity and displacement relations after release and explain why one common t is used.

answer.summary: a_x=0, a_y=-g; v_x=u, v_y=-gt; Delta x=ut, Delta y=-0.5gt², all at the same elapsed time t.
reasoning: After release only gravity acts in the ideal model.
Gravity has no horizontal component in the chosen frame.
Both component coordinates describe the same stone at the same instant.
answer.check: Horizontal velocity remains constant while downward speed magnitude grows with time.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit task is symbolic and model-based; no cliff height or numerical g is required.

microtopics.research_contribution: Selected ExamSIDE horizontal/oblique projectile questions justify a durable projectile model capability. Range, height and time-of-flight remain consequences/variations, not separate capabilities.

predict.prompt: Immediately after a horizontal launch, which acceleration component is zero in the ideal model?
predict.defensible_answer: a_x is zero; a_y is -g if +y is upward.

attempt.produces: A model declaration and component-equation setup for a horizontal or oblique projectile.

rubric.criterion: The learner selects gravity-only free flight, uses a_x=0/a_y=-g and one common time before calculating any named projectile quantity.
rubric.evidence_of: Projectile model selection rather than formula recall.

accepted: State assumptions, set component accelerations, then solve x/y with one t.
rejected: Start from a memorized range/height formula without establishing the free-flight component model.

route.ask: What forces remain after release in the idealized problem?
What are the horizontal and vertical component equations, and what clock do they share?
route.why_this_ask: Rebuilds the projectile specialization from 2D constant acceleration.

route.ask: What exact component condition identifies the event the question asks about?
route.why_this_ask: Separates model selection from event selection.

route.ask: If the event is the apex, what becomes zero and what definitely does not?
route.why_this_ask: Protects against the common full-velocity/full-acceleration zero shortcut.

route.ask: Does launch height equal landing height? If not, which shortcut becomes invalid?

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: Teaching states the projectile specialization; reconstruction derives it from the post-release interaction model and coordinate choice.

boundary_test.prompt: A launched object continues under significant horizontal thrust after release. May the standard a_x=0 projectile specialization be used?
boundary_test.answer: No. The object is not in gravity-only free flight; its horizontal acceleration is not zero under that model.
boundary_test.confirms: Projectile equations are conditional consequences of a declared force/model state.

relations.expression: v_x = u_x + a_x t; v_y = u_y + a_y t
relations.meaning: Each perpendicular velocity component follows the 1D constant-acceleration relation over one common interval.
conditions: a_x and a_y are constant over the interval.
Both component equations use the same elapsed time and frame.

derivation.action: Apply the existing constant-acceleration velocity relation v=u+at along the x axis only.
derivation.why_valid: The x component is one one-dimensional constant-acceleration motion when a_x is constant.

derivation.action: Apply the same relation independently along the y axis over the same elapsed time.
derivation.why_valid: The y component has its own constant acceleration a_y but describes the same event interval.

derivation.action: Read the two equations together as one velocity component pair at time t.
derivation.why_valid: The component pair represents one plane velocity only when frame and time agree.
derivation.output: v(t) has components (u_x+a_x t, u_y+a_y t)

limits: If either acceleration component varies during the interval, that component's constant-acceleration velocity equation is not exact over the whole interval.
These component equations do not by themselves select the coordinate frame or determine whether acceleration is constant.
checks: Units match velocity on both equations.
If a_x=0 then v_x stays constant; likewise for y.

relations.expression: Delta x = u_x t + 0.5 a_x t^2; Delta y = u_y t + 0.5 a_y t^2
relations.meaning: Each perpendicular displacement component follows the 1D constant-acceleration displacement relation over one common interval.
conditions: a_x and a_y are constant over the interval.
Both component equations use the same elapsed time and frame.

derivation.action: Apply the existing constant-acceleration displacement relation Delta s=u t+0.5 a t^2 to the x component.
derivation.why_valid: The x displacement is a one-dimensional component motion with initial velocity u_x and constant acceleration a_x.
derivation.output: Delta x = u_x t + 0.5 a_x t^2

derivation.action: Apply the same relation to the y component using the same elapsed time.
derivation.why_valid: The y component evolves independently but belongs to the same physical interval.
derivation.output: Delta y = u_y t + 0.5 a_y t^2

derivation.action: Recombine the two signed displacements as one plane displacement.
derivation.why_valid: A Cartesian displacement is determined by its signed perpendicular components.
derivation.output: Delta r has components (u_x t+0.5 a_x t^2, u_y t+0.5 a_y t^2)

limits: The displacement component equations require constant a_x and a_y over the interval on which each one is used.
They describe displacement from the chosen initial instant, not total path length.
checks: Setting one acceleration component to zero reduces that axis to uniform motion.

relations.expression: a_x = 0; a_y = -g; v_x = u_x; v_y = u_y - g t; Delta x = u_x t; Delta y = u_y t - 0.5 g t^2
relations.meaning: With +y upward, air resistance neglected and near-Earth constant g, projectile motion is 2D constant acceleration specialized to zero horizontal and downward vertical acceleration.
conditions: Near-Earth region with approximately constant g.
Air resistance neglected.
+y is declared upward for the displayed signs.
The object is in free flight after release.

derivation.action: For free flight near Earth with air resistance neglected and +y upward, set a_x=0 and a_y=-g.
derivation.why_valid: Gravity is the only retained acceleration in the ideal projectile model and points vertically downward.

derivation.action: Substitute a_x=0 and a_y=-g into the 2D velocity component relations.
derivation.why_valid: The projectile model is a specialization of the same component constant-acceleration equations.
derivation.output: v_x = u_x; v_y = u_y - g t

derivation.action: Substitute the same acceleration components into the 2D displacement relations.
derivation.why_valid: Horizontal and vertical displacements follow the same specialized component model over the shared time.
derivation.output: Delta x = u_x t; Delta y = u_y t - 0.5 g t^2

derivation.action: Check that horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical velocity changes linearly with time.
derivation.why_valid: Those trends follow directly from a_x=0 and a_y=-g.
derivation.output: constant v_x and linearly decreasing v_y under the declared +y-up convention

limits: The displayed projectile specialization is not exact when drag, propulsion, contact forces, appreciably varying g or a rotating-frame effect is material.
Changing the vertical sign convention changes the displayed signs; the physical downward acceleration does not change.
checks: At the highest point of an oblique trajectory, v_y=0 but a_y remains -g.
Both component equations use the same t.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_reference: Common PR #350 Motion in a Plane concept map; used as decomposition evidence, not source-question custody.

question_families.title: Motion in 2D component and projectile practice
solution_structure: Declare one frame, axes and one common elapsed time.
Choose or reject a constant-acceleration/projectile model before selecting equations.
Solve only the relevant signed x/y component equations.
Translate the requested event into an explicit component condition before solving for its time.
Recombine simultaneous components and check the result against the model boundary.

demand_dimensions.model_choice: Decide whether componentwise constant acceleration or the gravity-only projectile specialization is valid before applying it.
demand_dimensions.representation_translation: Convert a verbal or vector story into signed x/y states in one declared frame and common clock.
demand_dimensions.reasoning_steps: Choose the event condition, obtain its time from the relevant component, reuse that time across axes, and reconstruct the requested plane quantity.
demand_dimensions.novelty: Map horizontal launch, oblique launch, apex, same-height return and unequal-height landing onto the same component model without inventing separate physical laws.

safe_variations: Change signed initial components and acceleration components while preserving one frame and one clock.
Change the requested projectile event among apex, same-height return, unequal-height landing and specified later time while preserving gravity-only free flight.
Change launch from horizontal to oblique by changing the initial vertical component rather than changing the physical law.
transfer_boundaries: Do not use constant-acceleration equations on an axis whose acceleration component varies materially over the interval.
Do not use same-height flight-time or range shortcuts when launch and landing heights differ.
Do not use the standard projectile specialization when drag, propulsion or another retained force makes a_x=0 and a_y=-g invalid.
Do not duplicate relative-motion/moving-observer decisions in this bucket; those belong to the existing relative-motion capability graph.
common_wrong_routes: Give x and y different clocks for the same event.
Insert the acceleration magnitude into both component equations.
Set the whole velocity or acceleration to zero at the apex.
Treat horizontal launch as zero vertical motion for the whole flight.
Use same-height shortcuts for unequal-height landings.

questions.stem: A tracker reports x(t)=4t metres and y(t)=10-2t^2 metres for one particle in one fixed frame. Find the particle's position at t=2 s, and explain why x(2 s) may not be paired with y(3 s) to describe one position.
conditions: The two functions refer to the same particle and the same time coordinate.
Use the declared fixed x-y frame.

answer.summary: At t=2 s, x=8 m and y=2 m, so the position is (8,2) m in the declared frame. x(2 s) and y(3 s) cannot form one position because they refer to different instants.
reasoning: Evaluate both component descriptions at the same requested time.
A physical plane state is a simultaneous component pair.
answer.check: The answer must use one t for both components; mixing timestamps produces no real single-time state.

hints.text: What must be the same when x(t) and y(t) describe one particle at one instant?
Evaluate both component functions at the requested t before pairing them.

questions.stem: A particle starts with velocity (3 i + 4 j) m/s and has constant acceleration (2 i - 1 j) m/s^2 for 3 s. Find its velocity and displacement after 3 s.
conditions: Both acceleration components are constant over the 3 s interval.
The initial position is irrelevant because the question asks for displacement.

answer.summary: v=(9 i + 1 j) m/s and Delta r=(18 i + 7.5 j) m.
reasoning: Both axes use the same 3 s interval.
answer.check: Each axis uses only its own signed component values; units are m/s for velocity and m for displacement.

hints.text: Write the x and y initial velocity and acceleration values separately before calculating.
Apply the same 1D constant-acceleration relation independently on each axis using the common 3 s.

questions.stem: An ideal projectile is launched with already-resolved components u_x=12 m/s and u_y=20 m/s. Take +y upward and g=10 m/s^2. Find the time to the apex, the velocity at the apex, the acceleration at the apex, and the height gained above launch.
conditions: Air resistance is neglected.
After release, gravity is the only retained force.
The given initial components are already resolved.

answer.summary: The apex occurs at t=2 s. There v=(12 i + 0 j) m/s, a=(0 i - 10 j) m/s^2, and the height gained is 20 m.
reasoning: At the apex set v_y=u_y-gt=0, so t=20/10=2 s.
Horizontal acceleration is zero, so v_x remains 12 m/s.
Gravity still acts at the apex, so a_y=-10 m/s^2.
answer.check: Only v_y is zero at the apex; neither the full velocity nor the acceleration is zero.

hints.text: Which component condition defines the apex?
Set only v_y to zero, solve for the shared time, then evaluate the other requested quantities at that time.

questions.stem: A stone is launched horizontally at 15 m/s from a cliff 20 m above level ground. Take +y upward and g=10 m/s^2. Find the flight time, horizontal range and impact velocity.
conditions: Air resistance is neglected.
The launch has u_y=0.
Ground is 20 m below the launch point.

answer.summary: The flight time is 2 s, the horizontal range is 30 m, and the impact velocity is (15 i - 20 j) m/s.
reasoning: Use the vertical condition Delta y=-20=0*t-0.5(10)t^2, giving t=2 s.
Then Delta x=15(2)=30 m.
v_x=15 m/s and v_y=-10(2)=-20 m/s at impact.
answer.check: The fall time comes from vertical motion; changing only horizontal speed would change range but not the ideal fall time.

hints.text: Which component equation contains the known 20 m drop?
Find the common impact time from y first, then use that same time in x and in the velocity components.

questions.stem: An ideal projectile is launched and later lands at the same height with u_x=12 m/s, u_y=16 m/s and g=8 m/s^2. Find the total flight time, range and landing velocity.
conditions: Air resistance is neglected.
Launch and landing heights are equal.
Take +y upward.

answer.summary: The flight time is 4 s, the range is 48 m, and the landing velocity is (12 i - 16 j) m/s.
reasoning: At landing Delta y=0=16t-0.5(8)t^2; the nonzero root is t=4 s.
Horizontal velocity stays 12 m/s, so range=12(4)=48 m.
v_y=16-8(4)=-16 m/s at landing.
answer.check: At the same height, the horizontal component matches launch and the vertical component has equal magnitude with opposite sign.

hints.text: What vertical displacement condition is true at a same-height landing?
Use Delta y=0 to obtain the nonzero landing time, then reuse that time in x and v_y.

questions.stem: A particle is described verbally: at t=0 it is at the origin, moving east at 6 m/s and north at 2 m/s; during the next interval its acceleration is 3 m/s^2 south and zero east-west. Without being given component equations, choose a coordinate convention and write the signed component state that should be used for later calculation.
conditions: Use one fixed Cartesian frame.
The verbal directions must be translated into signed components before calculation.

answer.summary: One valid choice is +x east and +y north, giving u_x=+6 m/s, u_y=+2 m/s, a_x=0 and a_y=-3 m/s^2, all with one common t.
reasoning: Declare +x east and +y north.
Translate each direction into a sign in that frame.
Keep the same frame and clock for both component histories.
answer.check: Any consistently declared perpendicular axis convention is acceptable if all signs are transformed consistently.

rubric.criterion: Declares a single Cartesian frame before assigning signs.
rubric.evidence_of: Representation is chosen rather than assumed.

rubric.criterion: Translates east/north/south statements into consistent signed components.
rubric.evidence_of: Verbal motion is converted into canonical x/y state.

rubric.criterion: Keeps one common time for the two component histories.
rubric.evidence_of: Independent components are still one event.

adaptation.reason: Changes a ready-made component-function exercise into an unlabeled representation task while preserving one-frame/one-clock physics.

hints.text: Before writing numbers, which two perpendicular positive directions will you declare?
Translate each directional word into a sign only after that frame is fixed.

transfer.statement: The learner must convert a verbal direction description into signed x/y state without being handed the component representation.

questions.stem: Over 0<=t<=4 s, a particle has a_x=2 m/s^2 but a_y=3t m/s^2. Decide whether the ordinary constant-acceleration equations may be used exactly on x, on y, on both, or on neither over the whole interval. Explain the model choice before doing any further calculation.
conditions: The acceleration components are given as functions of time.
No numerical integration is required; the task is model selection.

answer.summary: The constant-acceleration equations are exact on x because a_x is constant, but not on y because a_y changes with time over the interval.
reasoning: Check each acceleration component separately.
a_x=2 is constant, so the 1D constant-acceleration x relations are valid.
a_y=3t varies with time, so the constant-a y relations are not exact over the whole interval.
answer.check: A constant total direction or a constant x component does not make the y component constant.

rubric.criterion: Checks x and y acceleration components separately.
rubric.evidence_of: Model validity is treated per component.

rubric.criterion: Accepts constant-acceleration equations only on x.
rubric.evidence_of: Does not let one valid axis license the other.

adaptation.reason: Changes a guaranteed constant-acceleration calculation into a model-validity decision.

hints.text: Is 'constant acceleration' one global label here, or must each component be checked over the interval?

transfer.statement: The learner must decide component-by-component whether the constant-acceleration model is valid instead of being told that it applies.

questions.stem: An ideal projectile begins 15 m above level ground with u_x=10 m/s and u_y=10 m/s. Take +y upward and g=10 m/s^2. Find the ground-impact time and horizontal range. Do not assume launch and landing are at the same height.
conditions: Air resistance is neglected.
Ground is 15 m below the launch point.
The initial velocity components are already resolved.

answer.summary: Ground impact occurs at t=3 s and the horizontal range is 30 m.
reasoning: Use the vertical impact condition Delta y=-15=10t-5t^2.
Solve 5t^2-10t-15=0, giving the physical root t=3 s.
Reuse t=3 s horizontally: Delta x=10(3)=30 m.
The same-height shortcut would use the wrong event condition here.
answer.check: Substitution into the vertical displacement gives -15 m; the nonzero same-height time 2u_y/g=2 s is not the ground-impact time.

rubric.criterion: Uses the actual vertical displacement -15 m rather than a same-height shortcut.
rubric.evidence_of: Selects the event condition from geometry.

rubric.criterion: Reuses the physical impact time in the horizontal equation.

adaptation.reason: Changes the landing geometry while preserving the same gravity-only projectile model.

hints.text: What vertical displacement identifies ground impact relative to the launch point?
Find the physical root from the y equation, then use that same time in x.

transfer.statement: The learner must replace the familiar same-height condition with an unequal-height event condition and carry the resulting time across axes.

questions.stem: An object is launched and, after release, a small rocket motor continues to provide a horizontal thrust that gives a_x=2 m/s^2 while gravity gives a_y=-g. Decide whether the standard ideal projectile specialization a_x=0, a_y=-g is valid and state the correct bounded model to use.
conditions: Air resistance is neglected.
The horizontal rocket thrust remains active after release.
The question asks for model selection, not a full trajectory calculation.

answer.summary: The standard ideal projectile specialization is not valid because a_x is not zero. Use the more general 2D constant-acceleration model with a_x=2 m/s^2 and a_y=-g for as long as those components remain constant.
reasoning: The standard projectile specialization requires gravity-only free flight.
The active rocket motor adds a retained horizontal acceleration.
Therefore use the parent 2D constant-acceleration capability rather than the gravity-only projectile specialization.
answer.check: If the motor is switched off after release and drag remains negligible, the standard a_x=0 projectile model becomes valid from that later instant.

rubric.evidence_of: Checks model conditions before formula use.

rubric.criterion: Falls back to the general component constant-acceleration model.
rubric.evidence_of: Chooses the smallest valid parent model rather than inventing a new law.

adaptation.reason: Changes a gravity-only horizontal-launch practice item into a post-release force-model validity decision by keeping horizontal propulsion active.

hints.text: Which post-release assumption makes a_x=0 in the standard projectile model, and is it true here?

transfer.statement: The learner must reject the familiar projectile specialization because one of its defining force/model conditions is explicitly broken.

questions.stem: An ideal projectile passes the same height once on the way up and once on the way down. Without calculating the times, compare v_x, v_y, speed and acceleration at those two events.
conditions: Air resistance is neglected.
Both events occur on the same trajectory at the same vertical position.
Take +y upward.

answer.summary: v_x is the same at both events; v_y has equal magnitude and opposite sign; therefore the speed is the same but the velocity vectors differ. Acceleration is the same (0,-g) at both events.
reasoning: Horizontal velocity remains constant because a_x=0.
At equal height in the same gravity-only trajectory, the vertical speed magnitude matches on ascent and descent, with opposite signs.
Combining the components gives equal speed magnitudes but different velocity directions.
Gravity gives the same downward acceleration at both events.
answer.check: The two velocity vectors cannot be identical because one has upward v_y and the other downward v_y.

rubric.criterion: Keeps v_x unchanged across the two events.
Gives v_y equal magnitude and opposite sign.
rubric.evidence_of: Understands same-height vertical-state symmetry without confusing vector equality.

rubric.criterion: Distinguishes equal speed from equal velocity.
rubric.evidence_of: Recombines components conceptually rather than comparing only magnitudes.

adaptation.reason: Changes a single apex-state calculation into a two-event equal-height state comparison requiring component invariants rather than event-time computation.

hints.text: At the same height, which horizontal quantity is unchanged throughout ideal flight, and what must differ between ascent and descent?
Compare component signs first; only then compare speed magnitudes.

transfer.statement: The learner must compare two equal-height events by component invariants rather than solve a routine time/range calculation.

teaching_routes.title: Reveal plane-motion component and projectile model
entry_needs: Signed vector components are available; one-dimensional constant-acceleration reasoning is available; angle decomposition is used only when a selected question supplies a magnitude-and-angle initial vector.
learner_actions: Separate one event into x/y histories with one clock.
Select the ideal projectile specialization before using projectile consequences.
help_plan: Draw a two-column x/y table with one shared t.
Transfer the existing 1D constant-acceleration relation to one axis at a time.
State post-release forces and coordinate sign before writing projectile equations.

when_not_suitable: Do not extend into calculus-based position-vector differentiation, drag, trajectory-equation derivation or advanced projectile geometry in this first slice.

teaching_routes.title: Elicit plane-motion component and projectile model
entry_needs: Learner can commit to an axis/model choice before seeing the completed component equations.
learner_actions: Explain what component independence does and does not mean.
Rebuild 2D constant acceleration from the 1D relation.
Derive projectile acceleration components from the gravity-only model.
help_plan: Ask what must share one time.
Ask which x quantities belong in the x equation.
Ask what forces remain after projectile release.
